Subject: TTFT & streaming cadence - recap from today

Alex — thanks again for taking time today. Quick recap from our discovery call and the items we promised to follow up on: 

Summary of requirements (as we heard them):
- Hard TTFT target: "Time-to-first-token" (TTFT) target of <= 120ms p95 for user-facing search/autocomplete flows.
- Streaming: real-time results via SSE or WebSocket, with small chunk cadence (aiming for 50–100ms between chunks for long responses).
- Throughput & concurrency: baseline of 200 concurrent active users (estimated 600 rps sustained, peaks to ~2k rps), requirement to sustain 500 concurrent model requests during peak.
- Latency SLOs: p50/p95/p99 targets for both TTFT and end-to-end token completion; desire SLOs surfaced per route.
- Quality: prefer open/quantized model family; acceptable trade-offs if TTFT/streaming cadence preserved.

Next steps we committed to:
1) Share a simple SLO worksheet and test plan (attached: slo_template.xlsx).
2) Ask you for representative sample payloads and target QPS patterns.
3) Propose an initial smoke test with our hosted infra, then run a Dedicated sizing exercise if needed.

Could you confirm the TTFT and chunk cadence numbers above and share sample payloads when you have a chance? We can then schedule a short engineering sync to align on telemetry and test harness.

Best,
Marissa

Thanks Marissa — that looks right. A few clarifications from our side: 

- TTFT: Our product team is comfortable with a goal of <= 120ms p95 for initial token for the autocomplete use case. For longer context (chat-style flows) we can tolerate 200ms p95.
- Streaming: SSE is preferred (we manage connections on the client side) but WebSocket is OK if it simplifies server routing. We care about chunk cadence more than chunk size — want sub-100ms cadence for the first 3–4 chunks, then steady 50–150ms for mid-stream updates.
- Concurrency/throughput: The 2k rps peak is for a marketing event. Typical sustained peak is ~600 rps. For sizing, assume 600 rps sustained and ability to burst to 2k rps for up to 10 minutes.
- Cold starts: must not cause TTFT spikes > 400ms for cold requests during bursts.

We will send sample payloads (100–200 representative requests) and a short CSV of traffic shapes by EOD Friday. Also, procurement wants to understand committed throughput pricing before we run a formal load test — can you share a Dedicated sizing & pricing PDF?

Thanks,
Alex
Head of Product, Finnect

Hi Alex — quick engineering note from our side on cold-starts and streaming behavior: 

- Cold starts: for hosted infra we mitigate with warm-pools and prefix/KV caching. For Dedicated we can provision pinned workers to avoid cold starts during event-driven bursts.
- TTFT drivers: model size, quantization, kernel selection and network RTT. For the 120ms p95 target on autocomplete we typically recommend: a smaller model family (or trimmed context window), int8 quant, and regional routing to reduce RTT.
- Streaming chunk cadence: SSE tends to add 3–8ms overhead per chunk vs raw sockets; most customers achieve ~40–80ms cadence on <1MB responses when we tune batch sizes and tokenization settings.

Reqs for smoke test: please include sample payloads with typical prompt lengths and the 90th/95th percentile length so we can configure batch/kv/cache sizing appropriately. Also include an estimated percent of requests that are prefix-heavy (e.g., large history) vs short prompts.

Connor

- 25% are mid-length (65–256 tokens) for feed generation; can tolerate 200ms p95 for TTFT.
- 5% are long history chat requests (up to 1k tokens). These are tolerance experiments — don't need streaming cadence sub-100ms.

Procurement: we can do the hosted smoke test first. After the smoke test we will review Dedicated pricing if we need pinned capacity. Procurement will review the PDF and follow up separately on committed throughput pricing.
